title: Explain the full flow of a microservices application (client → API Gateway → service discovery → service → DB → inter-service calls → response → logging/tracing).
shortTitle: Explain the full flow of a microservices application end to end
keyPoints: The client sends HTTPS to the API Gateway, which authenticates, rate-limits, and routes to the right service.
Service discovery resolves a logical service name to a currently healthy instance via a registry or DNS.
Each service owns its own database and runs business logic against it in a local transaction.
Inter-service calls use REST/gRPC (synchronous) or Kafka events (asynchronous), guarded by timeouts, retries, and circuit breakers.
The response flows back through the gateway; non-essential follow-up continues asynchronously via events.
A correlation ID propagated in headers stitches all logs and traces for one request across every service.
Distributed tracing (Jaeger/Zipkin) shows the request as a waterfall of spans so you can pinpoint slow hops.

s1_definition.oneliner: A request flows client to gateway to discovery to service to database, makes resilient inter-service calls when it needs another service's data, returns the response back through the gateway, and the whole journey is stitched together by a correlation identifier in structured logs and distributed traces.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **API Gateway** – the single secured front door that terminates TLS, validates the JWT, applies rate limiting, and routes the request to the correct backend service.
- **Service discovery** – a registry (Eureka, Consul) or platform DNS (Kubernetes) that resolves a logical service name to a healthy instance.
- **Database-per-service** – each service owns its data exclusively; no other service reads or writes its tables directly.
- **Inter-service calls** – synchronous (REST, gRPC) guarded by timeouts, retries, circuit breakers, and bulkheads; asynchronous (Kafka events) for decoupled flows.
- **Correlation ID** – a unique identifier propagated in headers across every hop so all log lines for one request can be gathered.
- **Distributed tracing** – each hop creates a span; parent and child spans are linked by trace context (W3C traceparent) and visualised as a waterfall in Jaeger or Zipkin.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh walks into National Bank of India to make a transfer. The security guard at the main door (API Gateway) checks his ID and points him to the correct counter. A directory (service discovery) tells the guard which counters are open. The transfer officer does the work using the transfer department's own files (database-per-service). To confirm details the officer phones the accounts department (inter-service call), with a timeout so he does not wait forever. The officer hands Rajesh a receipt (response), and every step is written in the branch logbook with the same reference number (correlation ID) so an auditor can follow the entire visit.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The full flow of a microservices application is the path one request takes from the client through the system and back. The client sends HTTPS to the API Gateway, which authenticates, rate-limits, and routes to the correct service. Service discovery resolves the logical name to a healthy instance. The service runs its business logic against its own database in a local transaction, and where it needs another service's data it makes a guarded inter-service call with timeouts, retries, and a circuit breaker, or publishes an event for decoupled flows.

The response flows back through the gateway, and non-essential follow-up like notifications continues asynchronously via events. Cutting across every hop is a correlation ID propagated in headers so all log lines for one request can be gathered, and distributed tracing shows the request as a waterfall of spans so you can pinpoint exactly which call was slow or failed.

At National Bank of India, Pankaj built this exact flow for transfers. The gateway authenticated and routed, discovery resolved one of several transfer-service instances, the transfer service did the debit and credit in a local transaction, and a circuit breaker saved them when the accounts service was overloaded during a deployment by failing fast with a cached fallback. The single most valuable thing they built was disciplined correlation-ID propagation, because the first time a transfer failed intermittently they found the slow hop in Jaeger in minutes.

Remember one sentence: a request flows client to gateway to discovery to service to database, makes resilient inter-service calls guarded by timeouts and circuit breakers, returns through the gateway, and is stitched together end to end by a correlation ID in structured logs and distributed traces.
